svg.aria-label: Azure application security groups: the three-rule worked example, why one rule exists only to undo a default, and the membership semantics and same-virtual-network constraints
svg.title: Azure application security groups: a three-tier policy written about roles rather than addresses, and the constraints that decide where the pattern works
svg.text: A three-tier policy with no addresses in it — and one rule spent undoing a default
THE SETUP: ONE NSG ON TWO SUBNETS, NO NSG ON ANY INTERFACE
AsgWeb — NIC1, NIC2
AsgLogic — NIC3
AsgDb — NIC4
A network interface can belong to several groups at once, up to the Azure limits.
Groups are created before the machines; membership is a property of the interface, not of the rule.
THE THREE RULES, IN EVALUATION ORDER — LOWEST NUMBER FIRST, FIRST MATCH STOPS
100 Allow-HTTP-Inbound-Internet
Internet → AsgWeb port 80 TCP Allow
110 Allow-Database-BusinessLogic
AsgLogic → AsgDb port 1433 TCP Allow
120 Deny-Database-All
any → AsgDb port 1433 Any Deny
The narrow allow at 110 is reached before the broad deny at 120, so business logic gets through
and everything else is blocked. No rule is needed to keep the internet off the inner tiers.
WHY ONE OF THE THREE RULES HAS TO EXIST AT ALL
AllowVNetInBound permits all communication between resources in the same virtual network, so
without the explicit deny the database accepts 1433 from everything the VirtualNetwork tag covers
— which includes every peered VNet and every connected on-premises range, not just these subnets.
A third of the example is spent on the platform’s starting posture.
WHAT MEMBERSHIP DOES TO A SUBNET-WIDE NSG
A rule naming a group applies only to interfaces in that group. A non-member is unaffected by it
even though the NSG is associated to the subnet.
So one NSG on one subnet can govern two neighbouring machines differently. The rule list and the
effective policy become different objects — read effective security rules, not the blade.
THE CONSTRAINTS THAT DECIDE WHERE THIS WORKS
· The first interface added fixes the group’s virtual network for life. Interfaces from a different
virtual network cannot be added.
· A rule naming a group as both source and destination needs both in the same virtual network —
so there is no group-to-group rule across a peering.
· One rule cannot name multiple groups, so three tiers reaching one database is three rules.
THE POINT
An address-based rule encodes a fact that was true at deployment. A group-based rule encodes an
intent, and survives every redeployment that would have invalidated the address.
Microsoft’s guidance: plan the groups in advance, and write rules with service tags or application
security groups rather than individual IP addresses or ranges, when possible.
Groups are an intra-VNet vocabulary. Across a peering boundary you are back to tags or ranges.
